# Life tables and the pricing of annuities (`life_tables_annuities`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/economy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Economy & finance (`economy`)
- Deps: helped by census_vital_registration, probability_statistics, compound_interest_exponential_growth, insurance
- Core idea: Follow a birth cohort, or calculate age-specific death rates using both deaths and population exposed at each age. Apply these rates to a hypothetical 1,000 newborns. The table gives the chance that a person of a given age lives another year, five, twenty. A life annuity (a yearly payment until death) is then worth the sum, over all future years, of the payment times the chance of being alive then, discounted at the interest rate. A 60-year-old's annuity is worth far less than a 10-year-old's. The same table prices life insurance and pensions and shows which ages and places have abnormal mortality.
- Pitfalls:
  - Selling annuities at the same price whatever the buyer's age: governments in England (1690s) and France lost heavily, and Geneva bankers profited by buying them on the lives of carefully chosen healthy young girls
  - Reading a life expectancy at birth of 30 as 'people died at 30': high infant mortality drags the average down, and those who survived childhood often reached their sixties
  - Building the table from a growing or migrating population as if it were stationary (Halley chose Breslau for that reason)
  - Forgetting interest: a payment due in 30 years is worth much less today even if the annuitant is sure to live
- History: rome: c. AD 220s – a table attributed to Ulpian (Digest 35.2.68) values life annuities by age for inheritance tax, without stated mortality data; europe: 1662 – Graunt's rough life table from the London bills of mortality; 1671 Johan de Witt prices Dutch life annuities by probability; 1693 Halley's Breslau table and annuity values; 1725 de Moivre; 1762 Equitable Society; 1815 Milne's Carlisle table
- Read:
  - Edmond Halley, An Estimate of the Degrees of the Mortality of Mankind, Philosophical Transactions 17 (1693)
  - Ian Hacking, The Emergence of Probability (1975)
  - Anders Hald, A History of Probability and Statistics and Their Applications before 1750 (1990)
